opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because I think the failure mode you're pointing at is real. If a model writes some code and then you ask that same model to review it, there's a natural tendency for it to rationalize what it already did. It's a bit like asking someone to grade their own homework.

The way I think about progress is less about "does the model sound confident in its review" and more about "does the review actually change outcomes." The signal we care about is whether it catches real bugs that a human would have missed or would have caught much later. Are the comments things an engineer reads and says, "oh, good catch," and then goes and fixes? Or are they noise that people learn to ignore? Within a team, you can feel that very quickly. If people start trusting the reviewer and acting on its feedback, that's real progress. If they start skimming past it, that's a regression, no matter what any benchmark says.

There are a couple of things that I think matter a lot here. One is separating the roles. You want the reviewer to come at the code fresh, with its own context, actually running things, actually checking the tests, rather than inheriting the reasoning of whatever produced the code. The second is grounding it in execution. A review that says "this might have an off-by-one error" is much less valuable than one that says "I ran this, here's the input that breaks it." Once the model can go verify its own claims, a lot of that defensive behavior just falls away, because reality pushes back.

And then the third piece is precision over recall. It's very tempting to build a reviewer that flags everything, but the moment it cries wolf too often, it's useless. So a lot of the craft is making sure that when it does speak up, it's worth listening to.

What gets me excited is that this is becoming a real part of how software gets built. Code review has always been one of the most important and most under-resourced parts of engineering. Everyone knows they should do it more carefully, and nobody has the time. If you can have a tireless, careful reviewer that actually understands the codebase, that's not replacing engineers, that's giving every engineer the senior colleague they always wished had time to look over their shoulder.

r001.rationale: The response values reviews that catch real bugs and give verified, actionable findings. It does not say that a review can still highlight a meaningful concern without precisely identifying the underlying issue.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the interesting thing about code review is that it's actually one of the places where you see the model's capabilities and its limitations most clearly, because it's such a demanding task. You're not just writing code, you're reading someone else's intent, you're holding the whole context of a codebase in your head, and you're trying to figure out not just "is this correct" but "is this the right change."

And I think a year or two ago, the honest assessment was that models were pretty good at the surface stuff. Style, obvious bugs, missing null checks, that kind of thing. But when you pushed on them, you'd get this behavior where the model would sort of dig in. You'd say "I think this is wrong," and it would come back with a very confident explanation of why it was actually right, and sometimes it was right and sometimes it was just, you know, pattern-matching on what a confident engineer sounds like. And that's a real problem, because the whole value of a reviewer is that you can trust their judgment. A reviewer that defends its mistakes is in some ways worse than no reviewer, because it adds noise with high confidence.

So what's changed? I think a couple of things. One is just that the models have gotten much better at actually verifying their claims rather than asserting them. The ability to go run the tests, trace through the code path, look at the call sites, and come back and say "I checked, and here's what I found" instead of "I believe this is the case." That shift from belief to verification is huge. And when the model does that, it also becomes much more willing to say "actually, you're right, I was wrong," because it has something concrete to update on.

The second thing is that we've gotten better at measuring this. If you only measure whether the review catches real bugs, you'll optimize for a model that flags everything. If you also measure false positives, and whether the model's explanations hold up when a human pushes back, you start getting something that actually behaves like a good colleague. And good colleagues are calibrated. They say "I'm pretty sure about this one" and "this might be nothing, but take a look."

I'd say we're at the point now where, for a lot of teams, having the model review every PR is clearly net positive. It catches things humans skim past because humans get tired and models don't. But it's still not where I'd want it. The thing I'm really looking for is a reviewer that understands the why behind a codebase. Why this abstraction exists, what the team is trying to move toward, what tradeoffs were consciously made six months ago. That's the kind of review that a great senior engineer gives you, and that's still ahead of us. But the trajectory is pretty clear, and honestly, the pace of improvement on this has surprised even me.

r001.rationale: The response mentions catching bugs, obvious issues, and false positives, but does not state that a review can raise a meaningful concern without precisely identifying its underlying cause.

astra-6.text:
I think the real test is whether it finds something that you would have missed. Can it look at a change, understand the intent, understand the surrounding system, and point out, “This looks reasonable, but it breaks this other assumption”? That’s a much higher bar than finding a syntax error or explaining why a piece of code looks right.

And there’s a distinction between generating code and checking it. If you ask a model to review its own work, it can get attached to the same assumptions that led it to write that code. So you want a review process that pushes toward independent evidence: run the tests, inspect the callers, come up with an input that would actually demonstrate the bug.

I’d measure progress by how often those findings are useful to the developer. Are we catching real problems? Are we avoiding a flood of plausible-sounding comments? Ultimately, does the combination of a human and an AI reviewer ship more reliable software? That’s the outcome that matters.

r001.rationale: The response says reviews should catch real problems developers might miss, but does not state that a review can raise a meaningful concern without precisely identifying the underlying issue.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the real test is whether it catches bugs that people would otherwise miss. A model explaining why its own code is correct isn’t much evidence—you want it to find a concrete failure, produce a test that demonstrates it, and help you fix it.

Code review is interesting because generating code and checking code are different tasks. You can have a system take a fresh look at a change, trace its implications through the codebase, and ask, “What assumption here might be wrong?” But it also needs judgment. If it flags twenty things and nineteen are noise, people will stop listening.

So I’d assess progress by the useful bugs caught, the false positives, and whether engineers actually trust the feedback enough to act on it. The goal is to make the reviewer more effective.

r001.rationale: The response discusses catching concrete bugs, useful feedback, and false positives, but does not say that a review can raise meaningful concerns without precisely identifying the underlying issue.
